summary: Field is a music production system that you drive from the command line. It has two parts that matter here. The field CLI is TypeScript, and field-audiod is a native audio daemon in C++ that plays, renders, and hosts plugins. The repository is about to go public, and a public repository with no license grants nobody the right to use, copy, or change the code.

This pull request licenses field's own code under MIT, with Amnesiac, LLC as the copyright holder. It adds the license text, declares it in package.json so npm and other tools report it, and adds a License section to the README. That section says what MIT does not cover. The daemon is built on JUCE, an audio framework whose version 8 is licensed under AGPLv3 or a paid commercial license, so a daemon binary built without the commercial license is covered by AGPLv3 as a whole.
No code changes. The review found one gap in the README section: the daemon also compiles in Steinberg's VST3 SDK, which has licenses of its own that the section does not name.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• MIT: a permissive license. Anyone may use, copy, change, and sell the code, provided they keep the copyright and license notice.
  • AGPLv3: a copyleft license. Anyone who distributes the program, or runs a changed version as a network service, must offer its source under the same terms.
  • GPLv3: the copyleft license AGPLv3 is based on, without the network-service clause.
  • JUCE: the C++ audio framework field-audiod is built on. The daemon pins version 8.0.4.
  • VST3 SDK: Steinberg's kit for loading VST3 plugins, bundled inside JUCE and compiled into the daemon for plugin hosting.
  • SPDX identifier: the standard short name for a license, such as MIT, that package tools read.

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html:
• One review, at 27188ee: changes requested, with one open finding on README.md line 175 about the VST3 SDK.
  • Three suggestions that do not block: spell the noun "license" as the rest of the repository does, give docs/architecture.md the same VST3 fix, and declare license = "MIT" in the three Python workers' pyproject.toml files.

groups.title: The MIT grant and the metadata that reports it
groups.kicker: The license text at the repository root, and the field that names it in package.json
intro: GitHub, npm, and other tools find a repository's license in two places. GitHub reads a LICENSE file at the root of the default branch and shows the license in the repository's About panel. npm and other JavaScript tools read the license field in package.json, which holds an SPDX identifier.

This group adds both. The text is the standard MIT license with the year and the holder filled in, so GitHub recognizes it. GitHub shows the license only after the pull request merges, because it reads the license from the default branch.

files.note: The standard MIT license, naming Amnesiac, LLC and the year 2026.

checks.text: The text matches GitHub's MIT template, fetched with gh api licenses/mit, word for word once the year and holder are filled in. The only difference is one trailing blank line in the template. The year 2026 is the year of the repository's first commit.

files.note: Declares the MIT SPDX identifier for the one package in the repository.

checks.text: The file parses with node, and pnpm install --frozen-lockfile passes at this head, because the lockfile does not record the license. No private or files field conflicts with the new one.
The three Python workers under python/ are field's own code too, but their pyproject.toml files declare no license, so uv and pip report none for them.

groups.title: What the MIT label does not cover
groups.kicker: The README's new License section, and the daemon binary it warns about
intro: MIT covers the code in this repository. It cannot cover the code that the build pulls in from elsewhere. native/audiod/CMakeLists.txt downloads JUCE 8.0.4 at build time and compiles its modules into field-audiod, so a daemon binary contains JUCE's code under JUCE's terms. In JUCE 8, every module is licensed under AGPLv3 or JUCE's commercial license. The README section says so, so that the MIT label does not suggest a built daemon is MIT too.

The same build also compiles Steinberg's VST3 SDK into the daemon, because the daemon hosts VST3 plugins. The SDK's interface files in JUCE 8.0.4 are licensed under GPLv3 or Steinberg's proprietary license, separately from JUCE. The section does not mention them, which is the review's open finding.

files.note: Adds the License section at the end: MIT for field's code, and AGPLv3 for a daemon binary built without a commercial JUCE license.

checks.text: The JUCE claim matches the source the build fetches. JUCE 8.0.4's LICENSE.md, and the header of every module the daemon links, from juce_core to juce_audio_processors and the GUI modules it pulls in, say AGPLv3 or commercial.

The section names JUCE as the only third-party license on the binary. JUCE_PLUGINHOST_VST3=1 in native/audiod/CMakeLists.txt also compiles Steinberg's VST3 SDK interface files into field-audiod, and in JUCE 8.0.4 those are licensed under GPLv3 or Steinberg's proprietary license. A reader who holds a commercial JUCE license would conclude that nothing else applies. The fix is either to name the SDK and its two licenses here, or to pin JUCE 8.0.11 or later, which bundles the SDK under MIT.
This is the only place in the repository that spells the noun "licence". The heading, docs/architecture.md, and the rest of the Markdown use "license".
